name: Tagoi
confidence_why: Bashir 2025 documents a lexical high/low tone contrast with minimal pairs from her own Tagoi field data, and Schadeberg & Elias 1979 independently record high/low tone, including tonal tense marking, in the Orig dialect, so the older view of Stevenson 1956-57 (reported in Tucker & Bryan 1966 and by Bashir) that stress rather than tone may carry the contrasts, which Stevenson himself hedged as "not fully investigated", is outweighed; no source states where word stress falls.

catalog_quote: Stevenson (1956/57: 47) himself doubted whether tone exists or, “apart from stress, plays an important role” in Rashad languages. However, data in the present contribution show evidence in favour of tone rather than stress, as will be discussed in SECTION 4. ... The issue of prosodic pitch, whether tone or stress, in Tagoi (or in other Rashad languages) has been the subject of different opinions. ... Stevenson instead claims that stress plays a marked role and may be responsible for grammatical and lexical contrast in Tagoi (Stevenson 1956/1957: 47; 1964: 86). The present contribution, however, attests evidence of a two-tone pitch contrast between high (H) and low (L) in monosyllabic and disyllabic nouns. Thus, it might be that Stevenson noticed the pitch distinction but he attributed it to stress. ... Recall that Tagoi has short and long vowels; both vowel/mora types bear tone. In a long syllable, the two vowels bear the same tone, either HH or LL, i.e., contour tones are phonemically non-existent

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tagoi is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language: lexical minimal pairs on mono- and disyllabic nouns (e.g. cɔ́r 'orphan' vs cɔ̀r 'moon'), tone borne by every mora, no phonemic contour tones (phonetic HL fall on word-final long syllables). The earlier claim (Stevenson 1956-57: 47; 1964: 86, followed by Tucker & Bryan 1966) that Tagoi/Rashad has dynamic stress rather than tone is explicitly rejected as a misreading of the pitch contrast. No source seen states a position for word stress; stress plays no role in the modern analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: a few nouns mark plural LL > LH together with final-vowel shortening (Table 11); phonetic falling HL only on word-final long syllables, never on monosyllables (Table 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/citation-form nouns (database of 800+ nouns elicited from four adult male Tagoi speakers in Khartoum, 2012-2022; Goy/Tagoi proper variety west of Rashad). Older group-level remark (Tucker & Bryan 1966 < Stevenson): 'Stress would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated' -- no placement given. Schadeberg & Elias 1979 (Orig dialect) likewise mark only tone (H/L) and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bashir 2025 describes Tagoi proper (Goy; ŋo-goi), spoken west of Rashad town, from speakers resident in Khartoum. Schadeberg & Elias 1979 describe the Orig (Turjuk, ŋóórig) dialect of the same language (tago1246; Glottolog lists Orig as a Tagoi dialect). Tutschek 1848/1850 describes Tumale (Umale), another Tagoi dialect. Tucker & Bryan 1966 / Stevenson 1956-57 treat the whole Tegali-Tagoi (Rashad) group together, i.e. including Tegali/Tagom (tega1236), which is a separate Glottolog language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57: three tone levels noted but no tonal minimal pairs found; stress 'would also seem to have some importance' but was not investigated, so no placement rule is given. The one placement datum recovered (p. 291) is that stress stays on the verb stem, not on the subject prefix, in both forms compared (yi-ko'rok 'I steal', yo-ko'rok 'I stole'); the vowel section says the reduced vowels I E O U occur in unstressed syllables but I and U are not confined to them.

Existing folder notes: Schadeberg & Elias 1979 describe the Orig/Turjuk dialect (tone only, no stress); Bashir 2025 describes Tagoi proper.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's classification 'tonal' (rule empty): Tucker & Bryan record lexical tone doublets for the group. It adds a substantive stress statement absent from the record: stress position (prefix vs stem) is reported as grammatically distinctive (Present vs Past) in TAGOI as well as RASHAD, with probable lexical stress classes of verbs in RASHAD. This is the Stevenson-derived 'stress' analysis that the catalog source Bashir 2025 explicitly reinterprets as pitch/tone ('it might be that Stevenson noticed the pitch distinction but he attributed it to stress'), so it is an analytic disagreement about the nature of the prominence, not a different placement rule; I keep 'refines'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Tegali-Tagoi (Rashad) group, second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57: tone is said to be of uninvestigated importance but lexical tone minimal pairs are recorded (RASHAD ris 'vein' vs ris 'cold', ye 'honey' vs ye 'egg', differing in tone marks); stress 'appears to have grammatical significance': the position of stress distinguishes Present from Past, illustrated for RASHAD (ome 'keyek 'the men eat' vs ome ke'yek 'the men ate') and for TAGOI proper (ye'yak 'I am eating' vs 'yeyak 'I ate'); in RASHAD verbs probably fall into lexical 'Stress Classes': type 1 stress on the stem in the Present and on the prefix in the Past, type 2 the reverse, type 3 stem stress in both tenses. No general word-stress placement rule (e.g. by syllable position or weight) is stated; everything is marked provisional ('appears', 'probable', 'not fully investigated').
new_statements.exceptions: The verb 'Stress Classes' themselves (types 1-3, cross-cutting the morphological classes I/II and A/B) are the stated variation; TAGOI 'eat' (ye'yak / 'yeyak: stem-stressed Present, prefix-stressed Past) patterns opposite to RASHAD 'eat' ('ye-yek / ye-'yek, type 2). Cross-reference to similar tense-linked stress shift in NUBIAN (p. 315), BEDAUYE (p. 502) and BILIN (p. 503).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's ch. 18b treats the 'Tegali-Tagoi Group' (Rashad) as a whole, with examples labelled RASHAD; statements are group-level and second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57, not specific to one Tagoi dialect (Goy, Umale, Moreb, Orig). Bashir 2025 describes Tagoi proper.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress placement: neither Tucker & Bryan 1966 (from Stevenson 1956-57) nor Bashir 2025 states where word stress falls. They differ on the tone inventory and on the status of stress: Tucker & Bryan report three tone levels with no tonal doublets and say stress 'would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated' (p. 290), while Bashir 2025 (already in the catalog) finds a two-tone H/L contrast and suggests that what Stevenson heard as stress was pitch. The p. 291 fragment 'Stress on Stem in both' (yi-ko'rok / yo-ko'rok) is the only placement-like datum and is compatible with both.
